x-ray: Before Wilhelm Röntgen, X-rays were noticed as an unidentified radiation coming from discharge tubes, by experimenters investigating cathode rays, the energetic electron beams first observed in 1869. Effects attributable to them appeared in many of the early Crookes tubes, invented around 1875. In these tubes a high direct-current voltage accelerated electrons so that they created X-rays when they struck the anode or the glass wall.

On 8 November 1895 Röntgen, a professor of physics, discovered X-rays while experimenting with Lenard tubes and Crookes tubes. On 28 December 1895 he submitted a preliminary communication, On a new kind of ray, to the journal of Würzburg's Physical-Medical Society, the first paper on X-rays. He called the radiation X to indicate an unknown type, and some early texts, taking the X for the Greek capital chi, speak of Chi-rays.

X-rays are electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths from about 10 nanometres to 10 picometres. Photons above about 5 to 10 keV are called hard X-rays and those of lower energy soft X-rays. There is no consensus on the boundary with gamma rays. One practice distinguishes them by source, X-rays coming from electron deexcitation and gamma rays from the decay of atomic nuclei, and another by wavelength.

X-rays are produced whenever charged particles of sufficient energy strike a material. The usual source is an X-ray tube, in which a high voltage accelerates electrons from a hot cathode into a metal target, the anode. In medical tubes the target is usually tungsten or an alloy of tungsten and rhenium. Bones show clearly on a radiograph because their calcium absorbs X-rays efficiently. Detectors were originally photographic plates and later film, and are now mostly digital.

Röntgen saw at once that X-rays could be used in medicine, and on 1 January 1896 he sent a letter to physicians he knew around Europe. The Scottish electrical engineer Alan Archibald Campbell-Swinton was the first after him to make an X-ray photograph, of a hand. By February there were 46 experimenters in North America alone. John Hall-Edwards made the first use under clinical conditions in Birmingham on 11 January 1896, radiographing a needle stuck in an associate's hand, and on 14 February 1896 he was the first to use X-rays in a surgical operation.

The hazards soon appeared, in stories of burns and hair loss. In February 1896 Professor John Daniel and William Lofland Dudley of Vanderbilt University reported hair loss after Dudley was X-rayed with an exposure of one hour. X-rays are ionising radiation and can cause DNA damage, burns, radiation sickness and cancer, yet the same property is used in radiotherapy to kill malignant cells. First-generation cold-cathode tubes of the Crookes type remained in use until about 1920.
xenophanes: The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius reports that Xenophanes was born in Colophon, a city of Ionia in present-day Turkey, and says he flourished in the 60th Olympiad (540–537 BCE). Modern scholars generally place his birth around 570–560 BCE. His surviving work refers to Thales, Epimenides and Pythagoras, and he is himself mentioned by Heraclitus and Epicharmus.

By his own account he was an itinerant poet who left his native land at the age of 25 and lived 67 years in other Greek lands, dying at or after the age of 92. Ancient testimony says he buried his sons, but little else about him or his family can be reliably established. His physical theories were probably influenced by the Milesians; his view that the rainbow is clouds may be read as a response to Anaximenes, who held that it is light reflected off clouds.

Xenophanes wrote a variety of poems, and his views are known only from fragments quoted by later writers. Diogenes Laertius says he wrote a poem of about 2,000 lines on the foundation of Colophon and Elea, and later testimony suggests his satires, called Silloi, filled at least five books. The title On Nature was probably given by librarians of the ancient world, and his remarks on natural philosophy were likely made incidentally in his satires. He composed elegiac couplets criticising traditional values of wealth, excess and athletic victory, and held that cultivating wisdom mattered more.

He criticised Homer and Hesiod for representing the gods as foolish or morally weak, and held that God is one, supreme among gods and men, and unlike mortals in body or mind. He sought natural explanations for clouds, rainbows and St. Elmo's fire. From fossils of sea creatures found above land he concluded that water had once covered the earth. He distinguished knowledge from belief, holding that an objective truth exists but that mortals cannot know it, and the sceptic Sextus Empiricus quotes his verses on the point.

Later ancient writers associated him with Elea, as founder of the Eleatic school and teacher of Parmenides and Zeno of Elea. Modern scholars generally find little justification for this, and note that no ancient writer expressly says he ever was at Elea. Timon of Phlius praised him as nearly a perfect sceptic, and the ancient tradition saw him as the first in a line leading to Pyrrhonism. He has been called the founder of epistemology, the first sceptic, an empiricist and a reformer of religion, while Karl Popper read him as a precursor of critical rationalism. Aristotle's Metaphysics summarised his view as the All is God.
xenophon: Xenophon was born in the Athenian deme of Erchia, the son of Gryllus, who belonged to an aristocratic family. The Peloponnesian War was fought through his childhood and youth. Like many wealthy young men of the time he associated with Socrates, and he probably served in the Athenian cavalry. He seems to have stayed in Athens under the Thirty Tyrants and to have fought the democratic insurgents in the civil war of 404 to 403 BCE. Xenophon was invited by Proxenus of Beotia to join the army that Cyrus the Younger was raising against the Persian satrap Tissaphernes.

Cyrus gathered a large army of Persians and Greeks, and the Greeks did not know at first that it was meant against King Artaxerxes II. After Cyrus was killed at the Battle of Cunaxa, the Spartan general Clearchus and four other generals were seized and executed on the invitation of Tissaphernes. The mercenaries, known as the Ten Thousand, then elected new leaders, among them Xenophon.

In the Anabasis he describes the retreat. The Greeks were harassed by Persian missile cavalry, fought the Carduchians in the mountains, forced a crossing of the Centrites River and marched through Armenia in winter without suitable clothing. They reached Trapezus on the Black Sea coast and fought the Colchians before making their way west. The military historian Theodore Ayrault Dodge called Xenophon the father of the system of retreat.

Afterwards Xenophon served with Spartan commanders in Anatolia and joined the campaign of King Agesilaus. Athens banished him for fighting on the Spartan side at the Battle of Coronea in 394 BCE. He received an estate at Scillus, where he lived for twenty-three years until the Elians confiscated it after Sparta's defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE. According to Diogenes Laertius he then moved to Corinth.

Xenophon's whole body of work survives. It includes the Hellenica, which continues Thucydides' account of the Peloponnesian War to 362 BCE and is partial to Sparta, the Cyropaedia, the biography Agesilaus, the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, and short treatises on horsemanship, hunting with dogs and the finances of Athens. His Socratic works are the Memorabilia, Apology, Symposium and Oeconomicus; apart from Plato's, they are the only surviving Socratic dialogues.

The Cyropaedia gives a fictional Cyrus the Great the qualities of an ideal ruler, and it differs from Herodotus on several points of his career. Some scholars read it as a warning that empires hold together only through a ruler of exceptional ability, and as a criticism of Athenian and Spartan ambitions for empire.
xerxes-i: Xerxes was born around 518 BCE, the son of Darius I and of Atossa, a daughter of Cyrus the Great. Greek sources describe the upbringing of Persian princes: raised by eunuchs, taught to ride and hunt from the age of seven, and given four aristocratic teachers from fourteen. It is unknown whether he learned to read or write. From 498 BCE he lived in the royal palace at Babylon.

When Darius prepared to go to Egypt in 487–486 BCE, Persian law required him to name a successor, and he chose Xerxes, his eldest son by Atossa, over Artobazan, who was born before Darius became king. Xerxes was crowned between October and December 486 BCE, at about thirty-two, and no one at court or among the subject nations is recorded as challenging him.

Xerxes put down a revolt in Egypt in January 484 BCE and made his full brother Achaemenes satrap there. Babylon rebelled at least twice: under Bel-shimanni in 484 BCE, a revolt that lasted about two weeks, and under Shamash-eriba from 482 BCE, defeated in March 481 BCE after a long siege. Afterwards Xerxes dropped the title King of Babylon and divided the large Babylonian satrapy into smaller units. Classical authors claim he wrecked the temples and removed the statue of Marduk, which the modern historian Amélie Kuhrt considers unlikely.

From 483 BCE he prepared the invasion of Greece, with a canal cut through the Athos peninsula and two pontoon bridges over the Hellespont. In 480 BCE he marched from Sardis. After Thermopylae and Artemisium he took and burned Athens, then lost the sea battle at Salamis. He withdrew with most of his army, leaving Mardonius, who was defeated at Plataea the next year. Back in Persia he finished works begun by Darius at Persepolis, including the Gate of All Nations and the Apadana, and built a palace at Susa.

In August 465 BCE Artabanus, commander of the royal guard, killed Xerxes with the help of the eunuch Aspamitres. Ctesias says Artabanus then blamed the crown prince Darius, while Aristotle says he killed Darius first. Xerxes's son Artaxerxes I took the throne. Xerxes held to Ahura Mazda as supreme deity, though scholars do not agree whether he was influenced by Zoroastrianism.

Greek and Roman sources present him largely in a negative light. Aeschylus's play The Persians (472 BCE) shows a hubristic ruler, and Herodotus gives a fuller portrait that Richard Stoneman reads as nuanced and tragic, while Pierre Briant calls it biased. He is identified with Ahasuerus in the Book of Esther, and is the hero of Handel's opera Serse (1738).
xhosa-people: The Xhosa are descendants of Nguni clans who settled in the southeastern part of Southern Africa. These farming agropastoralists brought cattle and goats, absorbed weaker San groups and formed chiefdoms and kingdoms, mainly in what is now the Eastern Cape. Archaeological evidence suggests that Xhosa-speaking people have lived in the area since at least the 7th century. According to oral tradition the Xhosa Kingdom was founded before the 15th century by Tshawe, after whom the royal clan is named, who overthrew his brother Cirha with the help of the amaNgwevu clan of the amaMpondomise Kingdom. Khoekhoe groups such as the Inqua and the Giqwa were incorporated and became tributary to the amaTshawe.

After Europeans settled the Cape in 1652 the Khoisan were gradually pushed eastwards, and by the 1700s the Cape Colony's borders had moved far enough east to create a hostile population ready to resist in the Eastern Cape. This began the Cape frontier wars, some of the longest military resistance to colonialism. Large parts of the native population were confined to reserves in the easternmost Cape, though they also continued to serve as labour inside the colony. These reserves were later renamed homelands and were dismantled in 1994.

In the 19th century the Xhosa fought off and took in many peoples fleeing the Zulus during the mfecane. The Xhosa called those they accepted amaMfengu, meaning wanderers, among them the amaBhaca, amaHlubi and amaZizi. Xhosa unity and their ability to resist colonial encroachment were weakened by the famines and divisions that followed the cattle-killing movement that began in 1856. Historians now see it as a millennialist response, directly to a lung disease spreading among their cattle and indirectly to the strain of losing territory and autonomy.

Cattle are important and the basis of wealth, and the Xhosa settled on the slopes of the Amatola and Winterberg Mountains, where the Kei and Fish Rivers and rich soils suit farming and grazing. Traditional foods include beef, mutton, goat, sorghum, maize meal, amasi, a fermented milk, and umqombothi, a beer of fermented maize and sorghum. Marriage, umtshato, involves a sequence of customs including the discussion of the woman's clan name, isiduko, since people sharing a clan name may not marry, and lobola negotiations, which were traditionally settled in cattle and are now often paid in money. The speakers of isiXhosa, a Bantu tonal language written in the Latin alphabet, understand Zulu to some degree.
xian: Xi'an lies on the Guanzhong Plain in the south-central part of Shaanxi province, on a flood plain made by eight surrounding rivers and streams. It borders the northern foot of the Qin Mountains to the south and the banks of the Wei River to the north. Hua Shan, one of the five sacred Taoist mountains, is about 100 km to the east, and the Loess Plateau lies not far to the north. The climate is temperate, influenced by the East Asian monsoon, with hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters.

The Lantian Man, discovered in 1963 in Lantian County 50 km southeast of the city, dates to at least 500,000 years before the present. Banpo, a Neolithic village found in 1953 on the eastern outskirts, contains the remains of several well-organised settlements carbon dated to 5,600 to 6,700 years ago.

The area became a cultural and political centre of China in the 11th century BCE with the founding of the Zhou dynasty, whose capital stood in the twin settlements of Fengjing and Haojing, together called Fenghao, southwest of the modern city. King Ping of Zhou later moved the capital to Luoyang because of political unrest. After the Warring States period the Qin dynasty, which ruled from 221 to 206 BCE, unified China from its capital at Xianyang, just northwest of Xi'an. Qin Shi Huang ordered the building of the Terracotta Army and his mausoleum, east of the city, almost as soon as he took the throne.

Under the name Chang'an, the city held the position of capital under several of the most important dynasties, including the Western Han, Sui, Northern Zhou and Tang. The present name, 西安, Western Peace, was adopted in 1369 under the early Ming dynasty. Jesuit missionaries recorded it as Si-ngan or Si-ngan-fou, after its status as a prefectural seat. The Qing dynasty set up a walled Manchu banner quarter in the northeast, on the site of the former palace of the Ming Prince of Qin, and a Han banner quarter in the southeast.

Xi'an is the capital of Shaanxi province and the most populous city in Northwestern China. It is counted among China's Five Great Ancient Capitals. The Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor with the Terracotta Army lies near it, and five component sites of the UNESCO-listed Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor are in the city. Chinese Standard Time is set by the National Time Service Center near Lintong.
xianbei: The Xianbei were probably not a single ethnic group but a multilingual confederation, made up mainly of Proto-Mongols and, to a smaller degree, Tungusic and Turkic peoples. They are said to descend from the Donghu, who split into the Wuhuan and the Xianbei when the Xiongnu defeated them at the end of the 3rd century BCE. In the 1st century BCE the Xianbei took part in the conflict between the Han dynasty and the Xiongnu, and they came to replace the Xiongnu on the Mongolian Plateau. In the mid-2nd century the chieftain Tanshihuai united the tribes, took the title Daren, or Elder, and divided his realm into three sections, each under an appointed chieftain.

By the Jian'an era (196-220) the Xianbei had divided into many groups. After the warlord Cao Cao destroyed the Wuhuan confederacy in 207, the fractured tribes began to pay tribute to the Chinese court. Around the turn of the 4th century, Xianbei and Wuhuan auxiliaries under Wang Jun fought in the War of the Eight Princes of the Western Jin dynasty and helped to capture Ye in 304 and Chang'an in 306, but also took part in the sackings. In the Sixteen Kingdoms period the Xianbei founded several short-lived states.

The Tuoba founded the Northern Wei after the collapse of the Former Qin. In 395 the Murong state of Later Yan was defeated at Canhe Slope, and within three years the Tuoba took most of present-day Shanxi and Hebei. In 493 Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital from Pingcheng to Luoyang, partly because Pingcheng had suffered drought and cattle plague in 487 and 50 to 60 per cent of its people had left. His policies suppressed Xianbei customs and promoted Han language, dress and rituals. A rebellion of six frontier garrisons in 524 led to the split of the Northern Wei into eastern and western regimes.

The Northern dynasties led or strongly influenced by the Xianbei merged with the general Chinese population by the Tang dynasty. Descendants of the Northern Wei royal family survived into the Tang, among them the chancellor Zhangsun Wuji and the poet Yuan Zhen, and the Sui and Tang governments and armies rested on institutions created by the Xianbei dynasties. The Xianbei language faded: the Book of Sui, completed in 636, records that many Xianbei of the Central Plains no longer understood it. Eighth-century Turkic inscriptions call China Tabgach, from Tuoba, and the Karakhanid rulers later used the title Tamghaj Khan.
xiangyang: Xiangyang stands at a strategic site on the middle reaches of the Han River, a major tributary of the Yangtze, which runs through the centre of the city and divides it north from south. The modern city is an agglomeration of two formerly separate cities, Fancheng to the north of the river and Xiangyang, also called Xiangcheng, to the south. What remains of old Xiangyang contains one of the oldest still-intact city walls in China. The two cities were merged in 1950 as Xiangfan, and the name Xiangyang was restored in 2010.

Xiangyang County was first established at the site of modern Xiangcheng in the early Western Han dynasty, and the name was used continuously for more than 2,000 years. In the last years of the Eastern Han it became the capital of Jing Province, and the warlord Liu Biao governed from here. Under his rule it became a destination for northern elites fleeing the warfare of the Central Plain. In the Battle of Xiangyang in 191 the rival warlord Sun Jian, father of Sun Quan, the founder of Eastern Wu, was defeated and killed. The Battle of Fancheng, two decades later, was one of the most important of the late Han and Three Kingdoms period and cost Liu Bei Jingzhou.

In the early Jin dynasty Xiangyang lay on the frontier with Eastern Wu. Its commander Yang Hu was remembered for a policy of border peace that allowed cross-border commerce, and the city accumulated supplies for ten years, which played a key part in the Jin conquest of Wu. After the Treaty of Shaoxing it became a garrison city on the northern frontier of the Southern Song. During the Mongol conquest of the Song, Xiangyang and Fancheng together formed one of the main obstacles to Mongol expansion, resisting for six years before surrendering in the Siege of Xiangyang.

In 1796 Xiangyang was one of the centres of the White Lotus Rebellion against the Qing, where the rebel leader Wang Cong'er organised an army of 50,000 and joined the main rebel forces in Sichuan. The revolt lasted nearly ten years.

Xiangyang is a prefecture-level city in northwestern Hubei, and the railways to Chongqing, Hankou–Danjiangkou and Jiaozuo–Liuzhou meet at Fancheng. It is the home of the Dongfeng Motors company. The city's boundaries in their present form date from 1983, when Xiangyang Prefecture was incorporated into Xiangfan City.
xianyang: Xianyang lay among the capital's environs under the Western Zhou and was made the capital of the state of Qin in 350 BCE, during the Warring States period. It was named Xianyang, meaning fully yang, because it lay south of the Jiuzong Mountains and north of the Wei River, both sunlit orientations. Under Duke Xiao of Qin the minister Shang Yang designed the city and organised the move of the administration from the old capital Yueyang. It remained the capital for over 140 years.

In 221 BCE Qin Shi Huang eliminated the six other warring states and established the first centralised empire in Chinese history. Noble families were compelled to move to Xianyang, and the weapons of the realm were gathered there to be melted into twelve towering statues. He expanded the city beyond its walls, built replicas of the palaces of the conquered states along the Wei River and a network of 300 palaces connected by elevated roads, and in 212 BCE began the Epang Palace. His lavish mausoleum, with the Terracotta Army, stood near the capital. These undertakings drew huge amounts of manpower and resources from agriculture and, together with repression, led to the fall of the dynasty.

After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE revolts broke out. In December 207 BCE the last Qin emperor, Ziying, surrendered to the rebel Liu Bang, who entered peacefully. Liu Bang had to hand the city to the more ruthless Xiang Yu, who killed Ziying and burned Xianyang in 206 BCE, destroying the only surviving copies of several banned books in the royal library.

Under the Han the part of Xianyang south of the Wei River was absorbed into Chang'an and the north became Weicheng County. Liu Bang, as Emperor Gaozu of Han, chose a high plain at Xianyang for his mausoleum, and many successors followed. Five mausoleum towns were established there and prominent families resettled in them, so that Wuling, the Five Mausoleums, became a name for the empire's elite. In the Tang period Weicheng held the first relay station out of Chang'an on the road to the western frontiers, and Wang Wei's poem A Song at Weicheng became a classic of farewell poetry. The present Xianyang was established in 1371, early in the Ming dynasty.

Xianyang is a prefecture-level city of Shaanxi, part of the Greater Xi'an Metropolitan Area, and the Xi'an Xianyang International Airport stands in it. Archaeologists have excavated many Qin sites there since the late 1950s, including palaces, workshops and tombs. The city has one UNESCO World Heritage Site and many Han and Tang imperial mausoleums, and it is the home of the Ban family of historians, Ban Gu, Ban Chao and Ban Zhao.
xin-dynasty: After the death of Emperor Wu of Han the ruling Liu family was beset by factional struggles, and the Wang family grew powerful under Emperor Cheng of Han. Its leading member, Wang Mang, acted as regent for several young puppet emperors and presented himself as a champion of Confucian virtues. After the death of Emperor Ping of Han in 6 CE he secured control of the empire and crushed rebellions in 6 and 7 CE. Two years later he usurped the throne and proclaimed the Xin dynasty, named for the fief of which he had been Marquess.

Wang Mang remade the Han government on his reading of the Confucian classics and of the ancient Western Zhou system. To weaken the nobles and help the peasants he redistributed land from the rich to those who owned none, limited the farmland a family could hold, taxed slave owning and prohibited the sale of slaves. He nationalised farmland, restored the state monopolies on salt and iron and replaced the gold currency with bronze. A 10% tax on the net earnings of gathering, fishing, herding and trade was abolished in 22 CE after it caused discontent.

Relations with the Xiongnu deteriorated, and Wang Mang kept 300,000 soldiers on the northern border, which drained the empire's resources. A change in the course of the Yellow River caused massive floods, and locust plagues and famines followed. Peasants in the east turned to banditry, and the strongest bands became the rebel armies known as the Red Eyebrows. They allied with discontented nobles and descendants of the Liu family, and by 19 CE there was a large-scale civil war.

Han restorationist armies completely defeated the Xin armies at the Battle of Kunyang in June or July 23 CE, and in October militias under Zhuang Ben and Zhuang Chun captured Chang'an and killed Wang Mang. In 25 CE Liu Xiu was crowned Emperor Guangwu of Han at Luoyang. He defeated the Red Eyebrows in 27 CE, and by 37 CE the Han dynasty was fully restored.
xingtai: Xingtai is a prefecture-level city in southern Hebei province, formerly known as Xingzhou or Shunde. It covers 12,486 km2 and borders Shijiazhuang and Hengshui to the north, Handan to the south, Shandong to the east and Shanxi to the west. The climate is continental and semi-arid, with hot, humid summers, cold, windy and very dry winters, and spring sandstorms blowing in from the Mongolian steppe. The city's rainfall averages 496.5 mm a year, more than half of it falling in July and August.

The history of Xingtai is traced back 3,500 years. It served as a capital under the Shang dynasty, and under the Zhou dynasty the State of Xing, from which the present name derives, was founded there. During the Warring States period the state of Zhao made it a provisional capital. It was known as Xindu for most of the Qin dynasty, but after the Battle of Julu in 207 BCE it became Xiangguo. When Shi Le of the Jie founded the Later Zhao in the Sixteen Kingdoms period, the capital was again at Xiangguo. Under the Sui and Tang it was called Xingzhou, and under the Yuan, Ming and Qing it was Shunde, a prefecture.

In Sui, Tang and Song times the area was the most prolific ceramics centre of northern China, rivalling the Yue ware of the south. The white ware and new techniques of the Xing kiln mark the transition from proto-porcelain to true porcelain. More than thirty kiln sites have been excavated in the city's districts. On 8 March 1966 an earthquake of magnitude 6.8, with its epicentre in Longyao County, struck the area, followed by five quakes above magnitude 6 until 29 March. It caused 8,064 deaths and destroyed more than 5 million houses.

At the 2020 census Xingtai had 7,111,106 inhabitants, and it administers 4 districts, 2 county-level cities and 12 counties. It is a base for natural resources in North China, producing 20 million metric tonnes of coal annually, and four railways and five expressways serve it.
xinhai-revolution: The revolution came after a decade of agitation, revolts and uprisings. The Qing had struggled to reform and to resist foreign aggression since its defeat in the First Opium War in 1842, and defeat by Japan in 1895 convinced many of the need for institutional change. The Guangxu Emperor's Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 was cancelled by a conservative coup led by the Empress Dowager Cixi. After 1900 conservatives at court thought the reforms too radical, and reformers thought them too slow. Anti-Manchu feeling, which had never entirely disappeared, fed the revolutionaries.

The flashpoint came on 10 October 1911 with the Wuchang Uprising by members of the New Army, after some Hubei units were sent to Sichuan to put down the Railway Protection Movement, a mass protest against the seizure of local railway ventures and their handover to foreign powers. Similar revolts followed, among them Changsha on 22 October, Taiyuan on 29 October, Kunming on 30 October and Shanghai on 3 November, and in the end every province renounced the Qing. Violence against Manchus occurred in several places. In Xi'an, after the Manchu quarter fell on 24 October, about 20,000 Manchus in the city were killed.

On 1 November the Qing court appointed Yuan Shikai prime minister. Revolutionary forces took Nanjing on 2 December, and a North–South Conference met in Shanghai on 18 December. On 29 December Sun Yat-sen was elected provisional president, and 1 January 1912 became the first day of the first year of the Republic of China.

Sun agreed to resign in favour of Yuan if Yuan secured the emperor's abdication. The edict of abdication of the six-year-old emperor was promulgated on 12 February 1912, and Yuan was sworn in as provisional president on 10 March. Song Jiaoren, who led the Kuomintang to a majority in the first National Assembly elections, was assassinated in Shanghai on 20 March 1913 under a secret order by Yuan. Yuan proclaimed himself emperor in December 1915 but abdicated in March 1916 after strong opposition, and his death in June 1916 was followed by decades of warlordism.

The revolution ended over two millennia of imperial rule in China. Tibet and Outer Mongolia took the fall of the dynasty as dissolving their allegiance, and Bogd Khan became ruler of the Bogd Khanate on 29 December 1911. 10 October is the National Day of the Republic of China on Taiwan and the Anniversary of the 1911 Revolution in China.
xining: Xining lies in the valley of the Huangshui River, a tributary of the Yellow River, at an average altitude of about 2,200 metres on the eastern edge of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. It is about 200 km west of Lanzhou and stood on the traditional main trade route from northern China into Tibet and the Qaidam Basin. It was a commercial hub on the Hexi Corridor caravan route, handling especially timber, wool and salt in ancient times, as part of the Northern Silk Road, whose use grew in the 1st century BCE after Han efforts to control it.

Under the Han dynasty a county called Linqiang was set up to control the local Qiang tribesmen. It was a frontier county again under the Sui and Tang, and in the 7th and early 8th centuries a centre of constant warfare with the Tuyuhun and Tibet. The Tibetans overran it in 763, and the Chinese knew it under Tibetan control as Qingtang. The Song dynasty recovered it in 1104 and named it Xining, meaning peace in the west; it has been the seat of a prefecture or superior prefecture under that name since then.

Tsongkhapa, founder of the Gelug school, was born in the region, and Kumbum Monastery was founded at his birthplace in the late 16th century, making Xining an important centre for the Gelug school. A magnitude 7.6 earthquake on 22 May 1927 killed over 40,000 people. Xining stayed in Gansu until 1928, when it became capital of the new province of Qinghai. Japanese aircraft bombed it in 1941, and the Salar general Han Youwen directed its defence. It received municipal status in 1945. Under Governor Ma Bufang it was industrialised and modernised, and the rail link to Lanzhou, completed in 1959, spurred industry.

Xining is the capital and most populous city of Qinghai and the largest city on the Tibetan Plateau, with about 2.5 million inhabitants at the 2020 census. Only about four of its roughly 37 nationalities are numerically significant: the Han, Hui, Monguor or Tu, and Tibetans. Kumbum Monastery, one of six leading monasteries of the Gelug school, lies to the south-west, and the Dongguan Mosque, over 600 years old, is one of the best known in north-west China. A railway reaches Lhasa, opened in 2006, and the city has a cool summer climate, which has earned it the name Summer Resort Capital of China.
xinjiang: Xinjiang is split by the Tian Shan mountain range into the Dzungarian Basin in the north and the Tarim Basin in the south. The Karakoram, Kunlun and Tian Shan ranges occupy much of its borders and its western and southern regions. Most of it is uninhabitable desert and dry grassland, and only about 9.7 per cent of the land is fit for habitation, mostly in oases at the foot of the mountains, where the cities lie. Its older English-language names include Chinese Turkestan and East Turkestan, and the Chinese called it Xiyu, the Western Regions.

Crossed by the Northern Silk Road, the Tarim and Dzungaria were known as the Western Regions. At the start of the Han dynasty the region was ruled by the Xiongnu. In the 2nd century BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent Zhang Qian west to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi, and in 60 BCE the Han established the Protectorate of the Western Regions at Wulei. The area, once inhabited by Indo-European Tocharians and Iranian Sakas who followed Buddhism and Zoroastrianism, became Muslim in the 10th century with the conversion of the Kara-Khanid Khanate, which held Kashgar.

The Uyghur state of the Turpan-Urumchi region submitted to Genghis Khan in 1209, and Xinjiang later came under Kaidu, a descendant of Ögedei Khan. In the 18th century the Qing fought the Dzungars for decades; Qing Manchu Bannermen then carried out the Dzungar genocide, nearly eradicating them and depopulating Dzungaria, and by 1759 China controlled both Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin. The two were governed separately until 1884, when the Qing established the province of Xinjiang. After the fall of the Qing in 1912, Yang Zengxin ruled it for the Republic of China until 1928. The region became part of the People's Republic of China in 1949 and an autonomous region in 1955.

Xinjiang, officially the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, is the largest province-level division of China, covering more than 1.6 million square kilometres in the northwest. It is home to the Uyghurs, Han Chinese, Hui, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Mongols and other peoples, with several autonomous prefectures and counties for minorities. Its largest cities include Ürümqi, Turpan, Kashgar and Karamay, and it has substantial oil and mineral reserves.
xiongnu-empire: The Mongolian Plateau of central and eastern Mongolia was earlier inhabited by the Slab Grave Culture, which lasted until the 3rd century BCE. The language of the Xiongnu is disputed, and Turkic, Iranian, Mongolic and Yeniseian origins have all been proposed.

Their first known leader, Touman, reigned between 220 and 209 BCE. In 215 BCE Emperor Qin Shi Huang sent General Meng Tian against the Xiongnu, who drove them from the Ordos Loop and forced them to flee north into the Mongolian Plateau. In 209 BCE Touman's son Modu became chanyu.

In the winter of 200 BCE, after a Xiongnu siege of Taiyuan, Emperor Gaozu of Han led a campaign against Modu and was ambushed at the Battle of Baideng, where he was cut off from supplies for seven days and narrowly escaped capture. Later the Han emperor Wu sent Zhang Qian west to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu. The mission failed, but his reports prompted Han preparations to break the Xiongnu hold on the westward routes.

When the chanyu Xulüquanqu died in 60 BCE, a succession dispute began that lasted until 53 BCE. In that year Huhanye moved south and submitted to the Han, entering tributary relations in which he was to pay homage, send a hostage prince and present tribute. His brother Zhizhi moved west and was killed by a Chinese army in 36 BCE near Lake Balkhash. A second succession quarrel around 47 CE left the Xiongnu divided into southern and northern groups. Those who resettled within the Great Wall gradually intermixed with the Han, and by the 7th century the Xiongnu had completely integrated into Chinese society.

The ruler was the chanyu, and below him stood the tuqi kings, of whom the Tuqi King of the Left was normally the heir. Beneath them were officials in left and right pairs and commanders of detachments of a thousand, a hundred and ten men, so that the nation was organised like an army. A weakness was the custom of lateral succession, in which a dead ruler's brother took power if his son was too young. The Xiongnu herded flocks and traded horses with China, and ate mostly mutton, horse meat and wild geese. According to the Book of Han they called Heaven Chēnglí, a transcription of Tengri.
xuanzang: Xuanzang was born Chen Hui, or Chen Yi, on 6 April 602 near present-day Luoyang in Henan, the youngest of four children of a family noted for its learning. After his father died in 611 he lived for five years with his elder brother, a monk, at the Jingtu Monastery in Luoyang, studying Mahayana and various early Buddhist schools. When the Sui dynasty collapsed in 618 the brothers fled to Chang'an and then to Chengdu in Sichuan, where they spent two or three years studying, including the Abhidharma-kośa Śāstra.

He later travelled through China looking for Buddhist books and reached Chang'an, then under Emperor Taizong of Tang. Like the earlier pilgrim Faxian, he was troubled by the incomplete and misinterpreted state of the scriptures that had reached China and by the competing theories in variant Chinese translations, and he sought original Sanskrit texts from India.

He defied his country's ban on travel abroad and made his way through Central Asian cities such as Khotan. In 630 he reached the kingdom of Agni, around Turpan, where a Buddhist king tried to persuade him to stay and equipped him with letters of introduction and funds when he declined. In India he studied at Nalanda with the monk Śīlabhadra. He left with Sanskrit texts carried by twenty packhorses and returned to China in 645. Emperor Taizong welcomed him but he refused the high civil appointments offered and retired to a monastery to translate.

With the emperor's support he set up a large translation bureau in Chang'an, drawing students from all over East Asia. He is credited with translating some 1,330 fascicles. His own strongest interest was Yogācāra, or Consciousness-only, which led to the Faxiang school, and his students Kuiji and Wŏnch'ŭk became influential authors.

In 646, at the emperor's request, Xuanzang completed the Records of the Western Regions. It is the longest and most detailed account of Central and South Asia by a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim and has helped to reconstruct the archaeological history of Bengal. It mixes first-hand report with hearsay and the implausible. His version of the Heart Sutra is the basis of Chinese commentaries and recitations across China, Korea, Vietnam and Japan. He died on 5 February 664 at Yuhua Palace in present-day Tongchuan, Shaanxi. His journey and its legends inspired the Ming novel Journey to the West by Wu Cheng'en, written about nine centuries after his death.
xuzhou: Xuzhou, also known as Pengcheng, is a prefecture-level city in north-western Jiangsu province. It lies at the junction of four provinces, Jiangsu, Shandong, Henan and Anhui, in a natural gap between the Shandong Hills and the North China Plain. It stands at the south-eastern end of the North China Plain, on deep alluvial deposits from the migrations of the Yellow River, and limestone hills rise abruptly from the floodplain, the highest of them Dadong Mountain at 361 metres. The city is the ancestral home of the Han dynasty imperial family and is rich in Han archaeological remains.

Archaeological remains in the region are largely associated with the Dawenkou culture. In the Shang dynasty a polity called Dapeng, or Peng, associated with the Dongyi, dominated the area, and it was subordinated to Shang authority after the campaigns of King Wu Ding. After Qin unification the region was organised as a commandery. During the collapse of Qin, Pengcheng became a centre of Chu revival: Emperor Yi of Chu moved his seat there in 208 BCE, and in 206 BCE Xiang Yu made it the capital of Western Chu. Despite his victory at the Battle of Pengcheng in 205 BCE the city passed to Han control, and in 202 BCE it became the capital of the Chu Princedom under Liu Jiao.

In 154 BCE Prince Liu Wu joined the Rebellion of the Seven Princes. After his defeat his Shizishan tomb nevertheless exceeded the usual limits and contained gold-threaded jade burial suits. After the Revolution of 1911 the railways completed in 1912 and 1915 made Xuzhou a junction and a recurring target for rival factions. General Zhang Xun used it as a base and held four Xuzhou Conferences in 1916 and 1917.

Xuzhou had about 9.08 million inhabitants at the 2020 census. Its modern coal industry began with the Jiawang Coal Mine in 1882, and for decades that was the only industrial-scale coal extraction in Jiangsu. Most local mines have since closed, and the city has become a centre of heavy machinery manufacturing. It is a major rail hub where the Beijing-Shanghai line meets the east-west Land Bridge corridor.
